extracted.intended_audience: scholars and students of humor research, psychology, linguistics, communication, and related disciplines
extracted.subtask_description: A general theoretical account of humor perception proposing three necessary and jointly sufficient conditions (V, N, and Simultaneity) and deriving consequences for types of humor, audience effects, intensity, and applications for interpreting others' laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: V: violation of a subjective moral principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The perceiver has in mind a view of the Situation as constituting a violation of a 'subjective moral principle' — i.e., some affective commitment of the perceiver to the way something in the Situation ought to be is violated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'violation' must be of a principle the perceiver cares about (an affective commitment). V is subjective (depends on perceiver and context); different individuals and cultures have different moral systems, so what counts as V varies. Examples/discussion: feminist listeners not laughing at sexist jokes (strong attachment to violated principle); sick jokes losing humor for a new parent who becomes more affected by the possibility. If no V interpretation is present, the situation can be unremarkable rather than funny.

rubrics_metrics.name: N: predominating view of the Situation as normal
rubrics_metrics.description: The perceiver has in mind a predominating view of the Situation as being normal (i.e., things are okay, acceptable, or non-aversive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘Normal’ is ambiguous (neutral or positive) but here marks the non-aversive evaluation opposite V. N must be present for humor; absence of N (e.g., an unambiguous moral violation) precludes humor and instead produces offense or threat. N can be driven out by a very strong V interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simultaneity: N and V present together
rubrics_metrics.description: The N and V understandings are present in the mind of the perceiver at the same instant in time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simultaneous presence (not sequential) of the two interpretations is required for humor perception; mere sequence of contrasting feelings yields a sequence of feelings (e.g., surprise then relief) but not humor. The order of external presentation of N and V is largely irrelevant so long as the perceiver ends up holding both simultaneously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity and joint sufficiency of the three conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: The three conditions (V, N, Simultaneity) are claimed to be individually necessary and jointly sufficient for humor perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If any condition is absent, humor will not be perceived (undergeneration would falsify necessity). If all are present, humor will be perceived (overgeneration would falsify sufficiency). The paper uses this as the core evaluative standard for what counts as humorous perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjective moral order: what counts as 'moral' in V
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'subjective moral order' consists of the set of principles an individual believes ought to hold and to which they have affective commitment; a violation of this subjective moral order constitutes V.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Morality is used empirically/broadly to mean the issues people actually care about (not necessarily philosophical ethics). A condition is moral here iff the perceiver thinks it ought to be a certain way and cares about it (shows affective response). This explains cross-cultural and individual differences in what is funny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative strength / predominance requirement (N must predominate over V)
rubrics_metrics.description: For humor to occur, the normality interpretation (N) must predominate (be felt as more consciously real or correct) relative to the violation interpretation (V).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If V is too strong (strong affective attachment to violated principle), N cannot be maintained and the perceiver is offended or threatened instead of amused. The relative intensity of N vs V explains why the same stimulus may be funny to one person, offensive to another, or unremarkable to a third.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-level scale of violations (no violation / funny violation / threatening violation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Situations can be classified along a three-level scale from 'no violation' (no V), to 'funny violation' (V present but N predominates), to 'threatening/ offensive violation' (V strong enough to preclude N).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains two meanings of 'That's not funny!' — either 'That's offensive!' (V too strong) or 'So what's the point?' (no V). The scale is used to predict responses and differentiate confusion, amusement, and offense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intensity / 'more is better' principle for perceived humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Perceived intensity of humor is governed by a 'more is better' principle: greater (appropriate) intensity of the relevant elements yields stronger humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper argues that increases in the strength of the relevant interpretations (when still allowing simultaneous N and V) increase perceived humor. This principle is used to explain variation in laugh intensity and some repetition effects (so long as N and V remain convincing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive elaboration and comprehension difficulty as contributors to humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Cognitive elaboration and certain comprehension difficulty can increase humor (further cognitive processing can enhance the humorous effect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The theory incorporates/comports with propositions that cognitive elaboration increases humor (Wyer & Collins). Comprehension difficulty is part of many humor phenomena; elaboration that yields maintaining or discovering the simultaneous N and V can enhance amusement. Repetition may reduce elaboration potential but can remain funny if N and V retain force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity, surprise, timing, aggression, superiority, and other recognized properties mapped to N/V interplay
rubrics_metrics.description: Phenomena traditionally labeled incongruity, surprise, timing, aggression, superiority, apparent comprehension difficulty, etc., are explicable as manifestations or mechanisms by which N and V (and their simultaneity) are produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper treats these as properties to be explained by the core three conditions rather than as independent necessary criteria; e.g., surprise helps pack two views into mind simultaneously, aggression/superiority relate to who is the object of the violation (self vs other).

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience design / tailoring jokes to listeners' moral viewpoints
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective joke-tellers must tailor their jokes to their audience's moral viewpoints (share or understand audience values) so that the audience will see the violation as acceptable while retaining a sense of normality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a speaker does not share or understand the audience's values, the humor may offend (V too strong) or be incomprehensible (no V). Speakers must avoid evoking too-strong or too-weak violations — a tight-rope walk on emotions; sociolinguistic 'audience design' is required for successful humor communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal distance and changing affective commitment
rubrics_metrics.description: Emotional involvement and affective commitment to a particular instance of violation change with time: something threatening in the moment can later be funny as personal involvement decreases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temporal distance is an independent measure of personal attachment; this dynamic explains why embarrassing or threatening events may become humorous in retrospect, and why long-term retrospection can render events unremarkable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Object of violation (self vs others) affects humorousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the violation happens to oneself or to others influences humorousness: people generally laugh more at violations that happen to others than at those that happen to themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because people care more about themselves, violations affecting others carry less affective weight and are more readily reframed as normal (N) in combination with V, producing humor (e.g., slapstick where others are hurt).

rubrics_metrics.name: Shared humor requires shared affective evaluations (high-quality communication)
rubrics_metrics.description: For humor to be shared and to serve communicative functions, participants must share (or at least understand) the relevant affective evaluations — the same or compatible subjective moral orders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shared humor implies mutual understanding and agreement about what is being violated; failure to share can lead to offense or confusion. This underlies humor's role in social bonding and its constraints in cross-cultural or generational contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic application: inferring others' moral commitments from laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Observing who laughs and who does not can be used as a fine-grained diagnostic tool to infer others' moral and emotional commitments (i.e., what principles they care about).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The theory suggests practical steps: if someone laughs where you don't, look for a violation they might care about; if someone doesn't laugh, consider which condition (N, V, simultaneity) is absent. Examples: driving anecdote where lack of laughter indicated strong commitment to safe-driving norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order irrelevance of presentation (but simultaneity in perception crucial)
rubrics_metrics.description: While the perceiver must hold N and V simultaneously, the formal order in which N and V are presented in a joke or stimulus is irrelevant to whether humor occurs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains why jokes that first present the violation then the normalizing framing (or vice versa) can both succeed; what matters is that the perceiver arrives at a simultaneous mental state containing both interpretations.
